analysis.one_liner: Caps interest rates on all consumer credit and limits lender fees to $15 with advance notice.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and died there when the 110th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Rep. John Tierney's bill would have amended the Truth in Lending Act to cap the annual interest rate on any consumer loan at 8 percentage points above the rate the IRS charges on underpaid taxes — a ceiling in the mid-teens at the time — and barred any creditor from charging more than $15 in fees. It also required credit card companies to mail or email a clear standalone notice 30 days before charging any fee, explaining why the fee would be charged and how to avoid it. The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers who pay credit card interest and fees. At the time, many credit cards carried rates of 20% or more; the bill would have capped them near the mid-teens and limited each fee to $15, while the notice rule would have given cardholders a 30-day window to avoid fees like late and over-limit charges.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households paying credit card interest and fees

how_it_helps.text: Caps the annual percentage rate on any extension of consumer credit at 8 percentage points above the IRS underpayment rate under Internal Revenue Code section 6621(a)(2), which was in the mid-single digits in 2008 — a ceiling in the mid-teens at a time when credit card rates commonly ran higher.
Limits any fee or charge a creditor imposes under the terms of a credit transaction to $15.

Bars credit card companies from imposing any fee — including annual, late payment, or over-the-limit fees — until 30 days after mailing or emailing the cardholder a standalone notice explaining how, when, and why the fee will be charged and how to prevent it.

analysis.who_pays: Banks, credit card issuers, and other consumer lenders, whose interest and fee revenue would be directly capped. Some higher-risk borrowers could also face less available credit, since lenders would no longer be able to price for that risk.

drawbacks.text: A hard interest cap set in the mid-teens applies to every kind of consumer credit, and lenders who cannot price for risk often respond by denying credit to weaker borrowers rather than lending at the capped rate — so people who most need access to credit could lose it.

The flat $15 fee cap covers all fees on all credit transactions, from a $35 credit card late fee to small-dollar loan charges, which supporters saw as protection but critics would call a one-size-fits-all limit that ignores differences among loan types and loan sizes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the millions of households carrying credit card balances, the caps would have delivered real, immediate savings on interest and fees, and the notice rule is a straightforward transparency win. The serious cost is on the credit-access side: a universal mid-teens rate ceiling means lenders would likely cut off or restrict borrowing by customers they could no longer price for risk. The bill never advanced far enough for those trade-offs to be examined in committee.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. John Tierney introduced the Loan Shark Prevention Act on September 18, 2008, near the peak of the financial crisis.
It was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day, and no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — was ever recorded.
The bill drew only one cosponsor besides Tierney, and the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers and other consumer lenders, who kept charging interest above the proposed cap and imposing fees without 30-day notice. No comparable national rate cap existed, so nothing changed for borrowers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Credit card issuers and consumer lenders

for.name: Rep. John F. Tierney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cap consumer credit interest rates at 8 points above the IRS underpayment rate, cap fees at $15, and require 30-day notice before credit card fees.

for.name: Rep. (cosponsor)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill — the only additional support it attracted in the House.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat with no committee action from its September 2008 referral until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Only two House Democrats ever backed the bill, and no vote was ever taken, so no partisan split on the merits is recorded.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers and consumer lenders
industries.note: The bill caps the interest rate they can charge on any consumer loan at roughly the mid-teens and limits every fee to $15, directly cutting interest and fee revenue — the core of their consumer lending profits. The 30-day notice rule would also let customers avoid fees like late and over-limit charges.
The rate cap applies to 'any extension of credit,' which would end the business model of charging triple-digit annual rates on small loans.
